If the position of an object relative to a spherical mirror is known, a ray construction can locate its **image**.
First construct the image of an individual point, using a ruler and compass to determine the reflected ray paths.
The focusing constructions below use the paraxial approximation.

To construct the reflected path of the incident ray $AC$, draw a secondary optical axis parallel to $AC$ (Figure 147).
This secondary axis meets the focal plane at $D$.
The line through the point of incidence $C$ and $D$ gives the reflected ray path.

The construction follows from the fact that paraxial rays parallel to the same secondary axis meet at one point in the focal plane after reflection.
Following just one of these rays is enough to locate that point.
Choose the ray through the center of curvature $O$, along the secondary axis itself.

This ray retraces its straight path after reflection, so its reflected path also passes through the unknown point $D$.
Thus $D$ lies in both the focal plane and the secondary axis: it is their intersection.
